lead: A memory chip is a grid of identical cells. The row decoder drives one wordline high; that row's cells place their bits on vertical bitlines; sense amplifiers decide each bit as 0 or 1. This one pattern covers SRAM, DRAM and ROM, though the cell and the read mechanism differ. It exists because a processor needs many words close at hand at nanosecond speed, and a regular grid is the cheapest way to store millions of bits. Every register file, cache, main memory and instruction ROM in a phone or a laptop uses it.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.5 for decoders, Chapter 4.6 for the storage loop and dynamic charge storage. Chapter 4.10 builds the decoders, column multiplexers and sense amplifiers around these cells.

sections.h3: The array, its address and its timing

blocks.text: Every memory is a grid of R rows by C columns of identical cells. The row decoder raises one wordline (WL); every cell on that row connects to its bitline (BL), or to a true and complement pair BL and BLB; the sense amplifiers turn the small bitline signal into full logic levels. An address of r row bits and c column bits picks one word: r bits choose one of 2r rows and c bits choose one group of bitlines from that row, so the array holds 2r+c words. How the address is split, and the decoders, column multiplexers and sense amplifiers themselves, are the subject of Chapter 4.10; this chapter is about the cell at each crossing.

Access time t<sub>AA</sub> is the delay from a new address to valid data. Cycle time t<sub>CYC</sub> is the shortest gap between the starts of two accesses. t<sub>CYC</sub> ≥ t<sub>AA</sub>, because after each access the bitlines must be precharged again and the old wordline must fall. A processor may request a word every cycle, so the array must meet t<sub>CYC</sub>. Mixing these two is a common error.

6T SRAM. Six transistors hold one bit. Two cross-coupled inverters (four transistors) form a loop; two access transistors connect the loop to BL and BLB, the true and complement bitlines. Read: precharge both bitlines to VDD, then drive WL high. The side of the cell that stores 0 pulls its bitline slightly down through the access and pull-down transistors. The sense amplifier resolves it. Write: the write driver drives BL and BLB strongly opposite; with WL high it overpowers the loop and flips it. When WL falls, the loop keeps the new bit. Read disturb: during a read the low internal node rises because the access transistor and pull-down transistor act as a divider. If it crosses the trip point, the cell flips. The cell ratio CR = (W/L of the pull-down) ÷ (W/L of the access transistor) keeps the read safe: a pull-down stronger than the access transistor holds the low node down, and textbook designs keep CR above about 1.2. Writing needs the opposite fight to be won: the access transistor must beat the pMOS pull-up, so the pull-up ratio PR = (W/L of the pull-up) ÷ (W/L of the access) is kept small, below about 1.8 in the usual textbook rule. SRAM is fast and needs no refresh, but six transistors per bit make it less dense and it leaks.

1T1C DRAM. One access transistor and one storage capacitor CS hold one bit as charge. Logic 1 is VDD on CS; logic 0 is 0 V. Read: precharge BL to VDD/2, drive WL high, and let charge share between CS and bitline capacitance CBL. The bitline moves by ΔV = (Vcell − VDD/2) × CS/(CS + CBL), where Vcell is the stored cell voltage before the read. The bitline is long and carries many cells, so CBL is several times CS; with CS/(CS + CBL) near 0.1 the swing is only tens of millivolts (worked example 2). The sense amplifier resolves it. The read is destructive: charge sharing removes charge, so the value must be written back (restore). Leakage drains CS, so every row must be refreshed within tREF, typically 64 ms. DRAM is dense and cheap per bit, but volatile and slower.

Mask ROM stores one bit at each row-column crossing by the presence or absence of a transistor: one transistor per bit. The row decoder drives a wordline; a programmed cell pulls its bitline low, a missing cell leaves it high. Mask ROM is programmed at fabrication, cheap in volume and non-volatile. PROM is one-time programmable by blowing fuses or antifuses. EPROM is erased by ultraviolet light through a quartz window. EEPROM is erased electrically, byte by byte. Flash is EEPROM-like but erased in blocks; it is the common code and SSD memory. A ROM is also a logic block: with the inputs on the address lines, a 2<sup>n</sup> × m ROM holds the truth table of any m functions of n variables. Programmable logic arrays share product terms instead of storing every minterm; see programmable logic devices and FPGA architecture.
Use SRAM for cache, DRAM for main memory, ROM or flash for firmware.

examples.question: A 256 Kbit SRAM is built as 1024 words × 256 bits. (a) How many address bits are needed? (b) How many cells are there? (c) A DRAM has 4096 rows and must refresh every row within 64 ms. Find the refresh rate in rows per millisecond and the interval between row refreshes.
steps: The word count is 1024 = 2<sup>10</sup>, so the address needs 10 bits.
Cells = 1024 × 256 = 262144 cells, which is 2<sup>18</sup> or 256 Kbit.
Refresh rate = 4096 rows ÷ 64 ms = 64 rows per millisecond.
Interval between rows = 64 ms ÷ 4096 = 0.015625 ms = 15.625 µs.
examples.answer: The SRAM needs 10 address bits and has 262144 cells; the DRAM refreshes 64 rows per millisecond, one row every 15.625 µs.
examples.check:
import math
words = 1024
bits_per_word = 256
addr_bits = int(math.log2(words))
cells = words * bits_per_word
rows = 4096
t_ref_ms = 64
rows_per_ms = rows / t_ref_ms
interval_us = t_ref_ms * 1000 / rows
print(addr_bits)
print(cells)
print(int(rows_per_ms))
print(interval_us)

examples.question: A DRAM cell has C<sub>S</sub> = 30 fF and its bitline has C<sub>BL</sub> = 270 fF. V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.2 V and the bitline is precharged to V<sub>DD</sub>/2. Find the bitline swing when the cell stores 1 and when it stores 0, and the cell voltage left after the read.
steps: Stored 0: V<sub>cell</sub> = 0 V. ΔV = (0 − 0.6) × 0.1 = −0.06 V = −60 mV.

After charge sharing the cell and the bitline sit at the same voltage: 0.6 + 0.06 = 0.66 V for a stored 1, and 0.6 − 0.06 = 0.54 V for a stored 0. Both are close to V<sub>DD</sub>/2, so the bit is gone until the sense amplifier drives the bitline to 1.2 V or 0 V and writes it back.
examples.answer: The swing is ±60 mV, and the cell is left at 0.66 V or 0.54 V, which is why the read is destructive and must be restored.

traps: Access time is address-to-data delay; cycle time is the minimum gap between two accesses. Cycle time is never smaller than access time.
A DRAM read shares charge with the bitline and destroys the stored value; it must be restored before the next access. SRAM read does not destroy the bit, but a poor cell ratio can disturb it.
Refresh interval t<sub>REF</sub> is the maximum time for all rows, not for one row. For 4096 rows and 64 ms, each row is refreshed every 15.6 µs while the whole array is refreshed every 64 ms.
ROM is non-volatile and needs no refresh; DRAM is volatile and needs refresh; SRAM is volatile but needs no refresh.

A stronger access transistor helps write but worsens read disturb; a stronger pull-down protects the read, and a weaker pMOS pull-up helps the write. SRAM cell sizing balances the cell ratio against the pull-up ratio.

quiz.a: A horizontal line driven by the row decoder; when high it connects every cell in one row to its bitline.

quiz.q: Which of SRAM, DRAM and mask ROM needs periodic refresh?
Why is a DRAM read destructive?
quiz.a: The stored charge shares with the much larger bitline capacitance, so the cell loses its value; the sense amplifier must write it back.

quiz.q: Why does a 6T SRAM need a cell ratio?
quiz.a: During a read, the access transistor and pull-down transistor form a divider that can raise the low node. A strong pull-down relative to access stops the cell from flipping.

quiz.q: A 512 Kbit SRAM is built as 2048 words. How many bits per word and how many address bits?
quiz.a: 512 Kbit = 524288 bits. 524288 ÷ 2048 = 256 bits per word. 2048 = 2<sup>11</sup>, so 11 address bits.

quiz.q: A DRAM has 8192 rows and t<sub>REF</sub> = 64 ms. Find the refresh rate and the interval between rows.
A 6T SRAM cell has a strong access transistor and a weak pull-down. What read problem appears, and how do you fix it without changing the bitline precharge?
quiz.a: Read disturb: the low node rises above the trip point and flips. Fix by widening the pull-down or weakening the access transistor to raise the cell ratio, while checking that write still overpowers the loop.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production memories are compiled: a foundry memory compiler stitches bitcells, sense amplifiers and redundancy into a macro with verified timing. Embedded DRAM and 3D stacked DRAM such as HBM trade cost for bandwidth. MRAM, RRAM and phase-change memory aim for non-volatility with SRAM-like speed. Search for SRAM read disturb cell ratio, DRAM refresh tREFI, and open-source memory compiler OpenRAM.
